questions.q: What are the three levels of government in India?
questions.a: The three levels are the local, state, and national (or central/union) governments. A wrong answer (e.g., naming only one) suggests the student is unaware of the multi-tiered structure of Indian governance.

questions.q: Why does a country like India need three different levels of government instead of just one?
questions.a: India is too vast and diverse for one group to manage every local detail; three levels allow for better focus on specific needs like local infrastructure versus national defense. A wrong answer suggests the student views government as a single monolithic block rather than a functional, divided system.

questions.q: If a new national highway is being built connecting Delhi to Mumbai, which level of government is likely responsible?
questions.a: The national (central) government, because highways connecting states fall under matters of national importance. A wrong answer shows confusion between local/state projects and national infrastructure.

questions.q: Compare the responsibilities of the local government with the national government. How do their scopes differ?
questions.a: Local government focuses on immediate community needs like street cleaning and local parks, while the national government handles major issues like foreign affairs and currency. A failure here indicates the student does not understand the "scope" of authority.

questions.q: Is it "better" to have only one powerful central government for the whole country, or is the three-tier system more effective? Why?
questions.a: The three-tier system is more effective because local representatives know local problems best, while the central government can focus on grand strategy. A student who misses this fails to appreciate the efficiency of decentralized governance.

questions.q: Imagine your local playground needs new swings. Who would you write a letter to, and why?
questions.a: The local government (municipality/panchayat), because it is a community-level issue. A poor answer (e.g., the President of India) shows a lack of understanding regarding local vs. national jurisdiction.
